binders: A triangular array p of nonnegative real parameters, with row N indexed by i in {0,...,N}.
A proof that every parameter p(N,i) is at most 1.
hypotheses: As N tends to infinity, the maximum of p(N,i) over i=0,...,N tends to 0.
As N tends to infinity, the sum of p(N,i) over i=0,...,N tends to the rate.
conclusions: As N tends to infinity, the probability law of the number of successes in the row of independent Bernoulli trials with success probabilities p(N,0),...,p(N,N), viewed as a real-valued random quantity, converges in the topology on real probability measures to the law of a Poisson random variable with the given rate, also viewed as real-valued.
mathematical_definitions: A Boolean configuration f has probability weight equal to the product over i=0,...,N of p(N,i) when f(i) is true and 1-p(N,i) when f(i) is false.
The row success count is the sum over i=0,...,N of 1 when f(i) is true and 0 otherwise.
The approximating law is the pushforward of the finite Boolean product PMF by the real-valued success-count map.
The maximum row parameter is the finite supremum of p(N,i) over all row indices.
The total row parameter is the real sum of p(N,i) over all row indices.
The limiting law is the pushforward of the Poisson measure on natural numbers by the natural-to-real cast.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For a triangular array of independent Bernoulli trials whose largest success probability tends to zero and whose sum of success probabilities tends to a nonnegative rate, the distribution of the number of successes converges to the Poisson distribution with that rate.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: Each row has N+1 coordinates, indexed from 0 through N.
Nonnegativity is enforced by the NNReal type, while the separate hypothesis p(N,i) ≤ 1 makes every parameter a valid Bernoulli probability.
The limiting rate is restricted to be nonnegative and may equal zero; at rate zero the limiting Poisson law is degenerate at zero.
The theorem constructs canonical finite product distributions directly and does not quantify random variables on a common probability space.
Both numerical assumptions are conditional hypotheses; an array not satisfying them yields no conclusion from the proposition.
The finite supremum is taken over a nonempty row because Fin(N+1) always has at least one element.
ambiguities: The dossier equips probability measures with the topology induced from finite measures but does not independently characterize that topology in probabilistic terminology; the conclusion is therefore stated using the supplied probability-measure topology, conventionally understood as weak convergence.
The independence interpretation is encoded by the product formula for Boolean configuration weights rather than by an explicit independence predicate.
